Let G and H be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order 21. By Sylow’s theorems, each has a unique subgroup of order 7, since the number of Sylow 7-subgroups divides 3 and is congruent to 1 modulo 7.

Choose a∈G of order 3 and b∈G of order 7. Then B=⟨b⟩ is normal. Also ⟨a⟩∩B={e}, so the 21 elements b^s a^r (0≤s<7, 0≤r<3) are distinct and hence comprise G. Normality gives

a b a⁻¹=b^k

for some k∈(Z/7Z)×. Since a³=e, conjugating b three times gives b=b^{k³}, so k³≡1 (mod 7). The roots are 1,2,4. If k=1, then a and b commute, making G=⟨a,b⟩ abelian. Thus k∈{2,4}.

Similarly, choose c∈H of order 3 and d∈H of order 7. Then every element of H has a unique form d^s c^r, and

c d c⁻¹=d^ℓ

for some ℓ∈{2,4}. Replacing c by c⁻¹ replaces ℓ by ℓ⁻¹ modulo 7; since 2⁻¹≡4 and 4⁻¹≡2 modulo 7, we may choose a generator c′ of ⟨c⟩ such that

c′d(c′)⁻¹=d^k.

Define φ:G→H on the unique normal forms by

φ(b^s a^r)=d^s(c′)^r.

For r,u modulo 3 and s,t modulo 7,

(b^s a^r)(b^t a^u)=b^{s+k^r t}a^{r+u},

and the identical formula holds in H with b,a replaced by d,c′. Therefore φ is a homomorphism. Uniqueness of the normal forms shows that φ is bijective. Hence G≅H. Since G and H were arbitrary, any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.

Let G be a nonabelian group of order 21. By Sylow’s theorems, the number n_7 of Sylow 7-subgroups satisfies n_7 ≡ 1 (mod 7) and n_7 | 3, so n_7=1. Thus the Sylow 7-subgroup P=⟨b⟩ is normal. By Cauchy’s theorem, G also contains an element a of order 3.

Because P is normal, conjugation by a induces an automorphism of P, so

a b a^{-1}=b^r

for some r∈(Z/7Z)^×. Since a^3=e, conjugating three times gives b=b^{r^3}, hence r^3≡1 (mod 7). The solutions are r≡1,2,4 (mod 7). If r=1, then a and b commute. Moreover, ⟨a⟩∩⟨b⟩={e}, so |⟨a⟩⟨b⟩|=3·7=21; hence a and b generate G, which would make G abelian. Therefore r is 2 or 4. Replacing a by a^{-1} replaces r by r^{-1}; since 4^{-1}≡2 (mod 7), we may choose a so that

a b a^{-1}=b^2.

Now let G and H be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order 21. By the preceding argument, choose generators a,b∈G and c,d∈H such that

a^3=c^3=e,  b^7=d^7=e,  a b a^{-1}=b^2,  c d c^{-1}=d^2.

Every element of G has a unique expression a^i b^j with 0≤i<3 and 0≤j<7: existence follows from |⟨a⟩⟨b⟩|=21, and uniqueness follows from ⟨a⟩∩⟨b⟩={e}. The same holds in H. Define

φ(a^i b^j)=c^i d^j.

This is therefore a well-defined bijection. From a b a^{-1}=b^2, we obtain

b^j a^k=a^k b^{j2^{-k}},

where exponents are taken modulo 7. Consequently,

(a^i b^j)(a^k b^ℓ)=a^{i+k}b^{j2^{-k}+ℓ}.

The identical multiplication formula holds for c^i d^j in H. Hence φ preserves multiplication and is a homomorphism. Since it is bijective, φ is an isomorphism. Thus any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.

Let \(G\) and \(H\) be nonabelian groups of order \(21\). By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow \(7\)-subgroup.

For \(G\), choose generators \(b\) of a Sylow \(7\)-subgroup and \(a\) of a Sylow \(3\)-subgroup. Their intersection is trivial, so \(G=\langle b\rangle\langle a\rangle\), and every element has a unique expression \(b^s a^r\), where \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\).

Since \(\langle b\rangle\) is normal, conjugation by \(a\) gives
\[
aba^{-1}=b^i
\]
for some \(i\in\{1,\dots,6\}\). Because \(a^3=e\), conjugating three times gives \(b=b^{i^3}\), hence \(i^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(i=1,2,4\). If \(i=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute and generate \(G\), making \(G\) abelian, a contradiction. Thus \(i=2\) or \(4\). In the latter case, replacing \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\) changes the exponent to \(4^{-1}\equiv2\pmod 7\). Therefore we may choose \(a,b\) so that
\[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

Applying the same argument to \(H\), choose generators \(c,d\) such that
\[
c^3=d^7=e,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2,
\]
and every element of \(H\) has a unique expression \(d^s c^r\).

Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(b^s a^r)=d^s c^r.
\]
This is well-defined by uniqueness of the normal forms. Since
\[
a^r b^t a^{-r}=b^{2^r t},
\]
we have
\[
(b^s a^r)(b^t a^u)=b^{s+2^r t}a^{r+u}.
\]
The identical formula holds in \(H\), so \(\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)\). Hence \(\phi\) is a homomorphism. It is bijective because it maps the unique \(21\) normal forms \(b^s a^r\) to the unique \(21\) normal forms \(d^s c^r\). Therefore \(G\cong H\). Thus any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.
